questions.question: Voyager 2, the only spacecraft to visit Uranus and Neptune, flew past them in 1986 and 1989. Astronomers call Jupiter and Saturn gas giants, but they call Uranus and Neptune ice giants. What sets the ice giants apart from the gas giants?
questions.answer: A bigger share of their matter is water, methane and ammonia
choices: A bigger share of their matter is water, methane and ammonia
A bigger share of their matter is the gases hydrogen and helium
A thick, solid crust of ice lies beneath their clouds
Their insides are frozen solid all the way to the centre
questions.context: Uranus and Neptune are only about a fifth hydrogen and helium; most of their matter is water, methane and ammonia, which astronomers call ices because they were frozen solid when the planets formed. Deep inside, those ices are a dense fluid thousands of degrees hot, so neither planet is frozen inside or has a solid surface. Jupiter and Saturn are more than nine-tenths hydrogen and helium.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade solar-system units sort the four outer planets into gas giants and ice giants by what they are made of.

questions.question: Galileo Galilei found Europa in January 1610, one of four moons he saw circling Jupiter through his telescope. Space probes have since shown that its surface is a bright crust of ice crossed by long dark cracks, with few craters. What do scientists think lies beneath Europa's ice?
questions.answer: An ocean of salty liquid water
choices: An ocean of salty liquid water
A deep sea of liquid methane
A thick layer of hot melted rock
Solid rock right up to the ice
questions.context: A spacecraft named Galileo found that the magnetic field around Europa changes in just the way a buried layer of salty water, which carries electric current, would make it change. That hidden ocean may hold about twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans, and since life needs liquid water, Europa is one of the best places to look for life beyond Earth. Seas of liquid methane lie on the surface of Saturn's moon Titan, and melted rock pours from the volcanoes of Jupiter's moon Io.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches the moons beyond our own, among them Galileo's four moons of Jupiter and the ocean thought to lie under Europa's ice.

questions.question: Giuseppe Piazzi, an astronomer in Sicily, spotted a faint moving dot on New Year's night of 1801 and named it Ceres. It lay in the wide gap between Mars and Jupiter, where a popular rule of the day said a planet should be. Within a few years more small bodies turned up in the same gap. What do astronomers now think these asteroids are?
questions.answer: Leftovers that never came together as a planet
choices: Leftovers that never came together as a planet
Pieces left from a planet that broke apart long ago
Rocks blasted off Mars by great impacts
Moons that broke away from Jupiter long ago
questions.context: The asteroids are rocky leftovers from the birth of the solar system, about 4.6 billion years ago; Jupiter's gravity kept stirring them up, so they never gathered into a planet. Heinrich Olbers proposed in 1802 that they were pieces of a shattered planet, a respectable idea in its day that astronomers have since given up. Ceres, the largest asteroid, is now called a dwarf planet.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches that asteroids are rocky leftovers in a belt between Mars and Jupiter, and Piazzi's 1801 find of Ceres is the usual first story.

questions.question: The asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter holds more than a million asteroids at least a kilometre wide, and the biggest, Ceres, is about 950 kilometres across. If all of them were packed together into one ball, how would its mass compare with the Moon's?
questions.answer: A few hundredths of the Moon's
choices: A few hundredths of the Moon's
About half as much as the Moon's
About the same as the Moon's
About twice as much as the Moon's
questions.context: All the asteroids together have only about 3 to 4 percent of the Moon's mass, and Ceres alone holds about a third of that. They are spread so thinly, on average nearly a million kilometres apart, that Pioneer 10 and many spacecraft since have crossed the belt unharmed. The crowded belts of films, where ships dodge rocks on every side, are nothing like the real one.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade units on the solar system's small bodies teach how little matter the asteroid belt holds and how far apart its asteroids are.

questions.question: Two small bodies swing in close to the Sun. One stays a bare, dark lump. The other grows a huge glowing head and a long tail, and astronomers call it a comet. What makes the comet change as it nears the Sun?
questions.answer: The Sun's heat turns its ice into gas
choices: The Sun's heat turns its ice into gas
The Sun's heat sets it burning like a torch
It sweeps up gas that lies near the Sun
Its rock glows red-hot in the Sun's heat
questions.context: A comet is a small lump of ice, rock and dust, a cosmic snowball. Near the Sun its ice turns straight into gas, which carries dust off with it to make the glowing head, called the coma, and the tail; nothing is burning, and the glow is sunlight on the dust and light from the gas. An asteroid is mostly rock and metal with little ice, so it stays a bare lump.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade sorts comets from asteroids: a comet is icy, and the Sun's heat turns its ice to gas to make the coma and tail.

questions.question: As a comet nears the Sun, a glowing tail streams out from it for millions of kilometres, pointing away from the Sun. What sends the tail in that direction?
questions.answer: The push of sunlight and the solar wind
choices: The push of sunlight and the solar wind
The trail the comet leaves behind as it moves
The Sun's gravity pulling hard on its head
The pull of the outer planets' gravity
questions.context: Sunlight pushes on the tail's dust, and the solar wind, a stream of charged particles flowing out from the Sun, sweeps its gas straight away from the Sun; the Sun's gravity pulls toward the Sun, never away. So the tail points away from the Sun even when the comet is heading back out, and then the comet travels tail first. A tail is not a trail left behind, the way smoke trails a moving train.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade lessons on comets explain why a comet's tail points away from the Sun: sunlight and the solar wind push it.

questions.question: Edmond Halley, an English astronomer, gathered careful records of comets from the past. He found that the bright comets seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 had crossed the sky on nearly the same path. What did Halley conclude about those three comets?
questions.answer: They were one comet that keeps coming back
choices: They were one comet that keeps coming back
They were pieces of one comet that broke apart
They were three comets passing through once each
They were three fires high in Earth's own air
questions.context: Halley worked out that they were one comet returning about every 76 years, and he predicted it would come back in 1758. He died in 1742, but Johann Georg Palitzsch, a German farmer and amateur astronomer, saw it on Christmas night of 1758, the first time anything but a planet was shown to travel round the Sun. Before then many people thought comets passed through only once on straight paths, and Aristotle had taught that they were fires high in Earth's air.
questions.grade_note: Halley's prediction that his comet would return is the first comet discovery story seventh-grade units tell.

questions.question: A pebble knocked off an asteroid drifts through space for millions of years. One night it plunges into Earth's air at tremendous speed and blazes across the sky as a streak of light. A small, blackened piece of it survives and lands in a field, where a farmer picks it up. Which part of this story is the meteor?
questions.answer: The glowing trail it draws across the sky
choices: The glowing trail it draws across the sky
The pebble while it drifts through space
The blackened stone in the farmer's field
The asteroid the pebble broke away from
questions.context: A meteor is the streak of light, often called a shooting star, though it has nothing to do with the stars. The pebble drifting in space is a meteoroid, and the piece that reaches the ground is a meteorite; most meteoroids burn up completely, so meteorites are rare. Most meteor showers come when Earth passes through dust a comet has left along its path, but the Geminids come from an asteroid, Phaethon.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade standards ask students to tell a meteoroid, a meteor and a meteorite apart.

questions.question: Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto in 1930, and for 76 years it was counted as the ninth planet. Then Mike Brown's team found Eris, a far-off world with more mass than Pluto. In 2006 the International Astronomical Union set rules for what counts as a planet, and Pluto became a dwarf planet. Which rule does Pluto fail?
questions.answer: It has not cleared its path of other bodies
choices: It has not cleared its path of other bodies
It is not massive enough to pull itself into a ball
It lies too far from the Sun to count
It travels round Neptune, not the Sun
questions.context: A planet must go round the Sun, be massive enough for its gravity to pull it round, and have cleared its neighbourhood of other bodies. Pluto is round and goes round the Sun, but it shares its zone of the Kuiper belt, the band of icy bodies beyond Neptune, with many others, so it fails the third rule. There is no rule about distance from the Sun, and Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake are dwarf planets too.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade units teach the 2006 definition of a planet and why Pluto, out in the Kuiper belt, became a dwarf planet.

questions.question: The Rosetta spacecraft set its lander, Philae, down on comet 67P in 2014; 67P goes round the Sun about once every six and a half years. Comet Hale-Bopp, which hung in the night sky for more than a year around 1997, takes about 2,400 years for one trip. Where did each of these comets most likely come from?
questions.answer: 67P from the Kuiper belt, and Hale-Bopp from the Oort cloud
choices: 67P from the Kuiper belt, and Hale-Bopp from the Oort cloud
67P from the Oort cloud, and Hale-Bopp from the Kuiper belt
Both of them from the Kuiper belt
Both of them from the Oort cloud
questions.context: Short-period comets such as 67P mostly come from the Kuiper belt, a flat band of icy bodies beyond Neptune, while long-period comets such as Hale-Bopp fall in from the Oort cloud, a vast, round shell of icy bodies thousands of times farther from the Sun than Earth is. Jan Oort, a Dutch astronomer, proposed the cloud in 1950 from the paths of long-period comets, and no one has ever seen it directly.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade units on the solar system's small bodies teach the Kuiper belt beyond Neptune and the far Oort cloud as the two homes of comets.

The stem opens on Voyager 2's flybys (F38, new). Key unchanged.

The choices are now a ladder of sizes, and the key, 'A few hundredths of the Moon's' (3 to 4 percent), is exact, so 'About half' cannot be read as 'much less'. Same fact (F16).

Stem and key unchanged, so the hash is the same.
